    {
      "startEvent": 1131,
      "endEvent": 1132,
      "contextStartEvent": 1093,
      "contextEndEvent": 1154,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "Well, there are artists and poets who think they're godless.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "Responding to godless artists as counterexamples, Peterson discounts their self-description instead of establishing that artistic creation requires belief in God (E1127–1132). Reclassification protects the necessity claim from this objection. His embodied account of belief (E1088–1092) supplies context, but does not establish the specifically religious dependence."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1152,
      "endEvent": 1154,
      "contextStartEvent": 1133,
      "contextEndEvent": 1219,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "But you act like you do.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "After Dillahunty renews his denial, Peterson treats refraining from violence as enacted God-belief, overriding that denial (E1152–1163). The missing bridge is why moral restraint specifically entails theism. He subsequently asks about value and punishment, but Dillahunty supplies a reciprocal-interest explanation (E1203–1219) that the affirmation itself does not address."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1224,
      "endEvent": 1228,
      "contextStartEvent": 1203,
      "contextEndEvent": 1233,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "It's like nothing's self-evident to the skeptic.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The maxim invokes skeptical identity to require justification of self-interest after reciprocal reasons have been supplied (E1203–1219). It could substitute an absolute characterization of skepticism for explaining the remaining inferential gap. However, Peterson explicitly frames the exchange as examining foundations (E1231–1233), and does not declare an answer inadmissible."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2077,
      "endEvent": 2081,
      "contextStartEvent": 1980,
      "contextEndEvent": 2081,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "I may not really need religion, but you people do.",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["shame"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Dillahunty paraphrases the preservation argument and rejects its presumed arrogance, potentially displacing the audience member's historical-dependence objection (E2061–2068) with a judgment about its advocate. Yet he already offers learning and transmission reasons (E2018–2033), and acknowledges religious usefulness (E2069–2076). Textual evidence does not clearly establish unconditional insulation from criticism."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2491,
      "endEvent": 2498,
      "contextStartEvent": 2360,
      "contextEndEvent": 2500,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "And there's nothing outside of the religious language that communicates that kind of grandeur.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "no",
      "emotionalDevices": ["comfort"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The categorical exclusivity claim supplies a conclusion stronger than the preceding account of religious narrative, meaning, and heroic exemplars earns (E2368–2490). Those reasons explain possible expressive value, but do not establish that secular language cannot provide comparable grandeur or consolation. No textual device makes contrary examples automatically inadmissible here."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2518,
      "endEvent": 2522,
      "contextStartEvent": 2506,
      "contextEndEvent": 2624,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment.",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "yes",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity", "fear"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Asked explicitly to justify excluding professed atheists, Peterson identifies the genuine atheist with Raskolnikov (E2506–2522), preserving that exclusion through a behavioral criterion. He supplies an extended literary and psychological argument (E2531–2624), so this is not slogan substitution. The protection concerns reclassifying nonviolent counterexamples, not the mere use of fiction or trauma."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 2833,
      "endEvent": 2852,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "without that being construed as evidence for the existence of a deity.",
      "explanation": "Peterson explicitly permits a materialistic account of intense deity experiences and acknowledges difficulty distinguishing the alternatives. This qualifies his earlier psychedelic argument rather than declaring every experience confirmation of an external deity."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1472,
      "endEvent": 1494,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "I'm open to revision on any of these at any time.",
      "explanation": "The surrounding account specifies revision when foundations conflict, appeals to observed human preferences, and allows better alternatives. His repeated 'getting better' language summarizes an articulated, qualified method rather than replacing reasons or excluding objections."
    }
